en: Supplement to the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, clarified by Deqing.
Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ratna*: "Laṅkā" is the name of the jewel; its full name is Śakrābhilagna.
This is called *nengsheng* (capable of conquering); its meaning is "firm and solid. *Abatuo* (avadāta) means "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
This indicates that this Laṅkā is an unsurpassed treasure. According to what I heard from a Brahmin teacher, this jewel has eight facets, yet it appears perfectly round when viewed;
its substance is luminous and translucent, and it is so extremely firm and solid that it cannot be pierced by drilling. Among all treasures in the world, none surpasses it.

Because the eye can surpass all things, it is called the "unsurpassed treasure. In the Western Regions and the South Seas, there is the Jewel Mountain of Laṅkā situated on the shore of the great ocean.
Since the mountain is composed entirely of this treasure, the mountain is named after it.
The mountain is five hundred yojanas high, and upon its summit is a city also named the Jewel City of Laṅkā. It has no gate through which one may enter, for it belongs to the Yakṣa King.

The basis for this is that the mountain’s shape is narrow at the base and broad at the summit; thus it is named "Inaccessible" (Abhigamana), for only those possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) can enter.
This is the origin of this sutra: the Buddha, having preached the Dharma in the dragon palace within the great ocean for seven days, returned and passed beneath the mountain.
Looking back, he addressed the assembly, saying: "All Buddhas of the past have, at this very mountain, expounded the realm of their own realization; I, too, shall now do so."
At that time, because the Yakṣa King Śaila perceived the Buddha’s words through his supernormal power, he went to invite the Buddha to enter the city to expound this sutra.

Thus, "Śaila" (Mountain-Eye) refers to the name of the person, while "Ratnaprabhāsa" (Jewel-Brightness) refers to the name of the location; taking both together as a metaphor, they form the title of the work.
Furthermore, when explaining the sutra solely by means of this metaphor, the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) Tathāgatagarbha-citta is also called "Jewel-Brightness."

The wondrous nature; it is also called the precious, enlightened, and luminous mind. This is the substance of the unshakable wisdom of the firm *dharmakāya*, named the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvidita-āryajñāna*).

It is the quiescent single mind, named the great ocean of quiescent extinction (*mahāśānti-samudra*), also called the ocean of wisdom, the ocean of awakening, or the ocean of precious luminosity and emptiness.

As the subsequent scripture states, it is the "ocean of the storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna-samudra*), meaning that sentient beings inherently possess the pure *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Deluded, it becomes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); consciousness transforms into sentient beings composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Self-awakened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) transforms into false conceptualization and afflictions (*kleśa*).
The jewel-bright ocean of emptiness becomes the karmic ocean of birth and death. A yakṣa is a malevolent ghost that flies about and eats human flesh;
thus, though the mountain is five hundred *yojanas* high and dwells in the midst of the great ocean, it acts as an affliction.

This is the realm occupied by the *yakṣas* of birth and death. When the Buddha dwells upon this mountain and speaks of the realm of self-realization (*svasaṃvedya-viṣaya*), he refers to the noble wisdom of personal awakening (*ārya-pratyātma-jñāna*) with which one observes the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*. Birth and death are themselves *nirvāṇa*; afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves *bodhi*.
The present five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), body, and mind are themselves the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata. One suddenly realizes the single mind; furthermore...
There is no separate dharma; this is the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna). It is not a realm of mental consciousness or discursive thought.

It is permitted only for those of the highest faculties to realize it suddenly and all at once; if they do not realize it, it is not permitted, because the consciousness would otherwise settle upon it. Thus, the mountain is called "Inaccessible."
Only those possessing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are able to enter it. "Jewel" refers to the unsurpassed jewel; "place" refers to a place where one cannot go.

This serves as a metaphor for this sutra’s revelation of the ultimate mind (*paramārtha-citta*), which transcends the realms of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*), and is thus the unsurpassed Dharma-gate.

This sutra elucidates that the five dharmas (*pañca-dharma*), the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), and the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*) are all empty, along with the two absences (*dvaya-nairātmya*).
I shall explain both together. This directly reveals the transcendence of the realms of mind, thought, and consciousness;
therefore, Dharmatrāta pointed to this as the "Mind-Seal" (*cittamudrā*). Thus, the essential purport of the entire sutra lies within this single title.

The metaphorical elucidation and the account of the origins of the Yakṣa King have already exhausted its profound and wondrous meaning. According to Tiantai’s fivefold method of interpreting titles, the title of this sutra is singular.
The metaphor is "name. Its essence is the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which is quiescent and of one mind. Its tenet is the noble wisdom of self-awakening.

Because it is specifically intended to refute the false attachments of the two vehicles and non-Buddhists, its function is designated as "subduing the heterodox and revealing the orthodox. Its doctrinal characteristic is designated as the Unsurpassed Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna.
By means of this sūtra, it is revealed that the five natures, the three vehicles, those without nature, and icchantikas are all permitted [to attain enlightenment].
He attains Buddhahood. Because this [text] serves as the vanguard for the revelation and clarification of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is judged to be its precursor.

As for the "Chapter on the Buddha-Speech Mind" (*Buddhabhāṣita-citta-paṭala*), this scripture takes the direct pointing to the quiescent single mind as its central tenet and the realization through the noble wisdom of self-awakening as its goal.

Since this mind does not belong to delusion or enlightenment and transcends the distinction between sages and ordinary beings, it encompasses the ten realms of existence, including both the environment and the sentient beings therein.

Regarding cause and effect, not a single dharma is established; that is to say, the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty, and the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness are both discarded.
Since these four gates pertain to the boundaries of delusion and enlightenment, Mahāmati praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
"Whether existent or non-existent, one is free from both extremes. This is because existence refers to the phenomena of saṃsāra, and non-existence refers to the phenomena of nirvāṇa.
When both of these are transcended, the nature of the *dharmadhātu*—empty, quiescent, and the single mind—is revealed.

Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Mind-Essence of the Buddha's Words," meaning that what the Buddha taught is solely this one mind-dharma. Thus, the Chan school points to this as the "Mind Seal" (*cittamudrā*).
This is called the supreme path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna.
Mahāmati’s five and a half verses in praise of the Buddha exhaustively elucidate the purport of the One Mind. Therefore, the subsequent passage revealing the One Mind states:
Emptiness is non-arising and non-dual, because it is free from the characteristics of intrinsic nature. The first verse states: "The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky.
This praises the Buddha’s ability to realize the truth of the emptiness of the one mind, clarifying that the imagined nature is fundamentally non-existent.

The term "world" (*loka*) encompasses the three worlds: the world of the wise and perfectly awakened ones (*jñāna-sambuddha-loka*), the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), and the world of the physical environment (*bhājana-loka*).

These collectively comprise the ten dharma-realms, including both the primary and secondary causes and effects. When these three worlds are viewed as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, they are called the "threefold world.

However, when viewed as manifestations of the mind alone, they are fundamentally without arising or ceasing; they exist only through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), for their nature is empty.
Therefore, it is like flowers in the sky. This single verse already transcends the causes and effects of delusion and enlightenment, directly pointing to the source of the one mind.
Only the Buddha’s eye of self-realized noble wisdom can fully realize this mind; thus it is said that wisdom cannot apprehend the marks of existence or non-existence.
Now, out of compassion for sentient beings who are deluded regarding this, he manifests in the world through his great compassion of identical essence to reveal and instruct the multitude.
Because it arises, it is said that "the mind of great compassion is aroused. Thus, what is now being taught is precisely to demonstrate this single mind.
The subsequent verse states: "All phenomena are like illusions; they are far removed from mind and consciousness. This demonstrates the meaning that the single mind is fundamentally without arising.

Together with the following verse, it clarifies that the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is devoid of intrinsic nature and exists only through conditions. The intent is as follows: the world...
Since there is currently arising and ceasing within the interval, why do you say it is empty? Therefore, it is said that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning;

they exist only through dependence on others, and are thus like illusions. The analogy of illusion indicates that arising is fundamentally non-arising. If one’s deluded mind engages in conceptual discrimination, one perceives arising and ceasing;
if one distances oneself from the discrimination of mind and consciousness so that they do not arise, then the very substance of things is non-arising. One realizes their total absence.
If even a single phenomenon accords with one's own mind, is it not empty?
Following the pattern of the three verses, the text should state: "The world is always like a dream, far removed from annihilation and permanence. This reveals non-duality.
The meaning is that all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds are manifestations of the mind alone; [yet] the heterodox and the followers of the Two Vehicles do not...

One realizes that [phenomena] arise based on the dependent nature of mind-only; thus, one falsely discriminates between existence and non-existence, giving rise to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
If one realizes mind-only, then one remains far removed from annihilationism and eternalism, and realizes the absence of these two views.

These four verses reveal the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The intended meaning is as follows: if sentient beings do not realize that all is but mind-only (*cittamātra*), they falsely cling to the two selves of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ātman*).
This serves as the root of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*); consequently, they give rise to delusions and create karma, falsely perceiving the marks of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Once they realize that all is but mind-only, both person and phenomena are simultaneously forgotten; the two obstacles are instantly purified, and there remains only the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Thus, the marks of birth and death no longer [arise].
This can be understood. These four preceding verses praise the Buddha’s transcendence of the mundane world and the phenomena of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

However, because [the Buddha] is empty, unarisen, non-dual, and free from the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this accords with the intent of "single-mindedness" (*ekacitta*) in this sutra, as will become clear in the subsequent text.
As for the explanation based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), this follows the intention of Qingliang; therefore, I have cited these topical headings (*yiming*) to corroborate the meaning.
The five verses praise the Buddha as transcending the dharma of *nirvāṇa*. The intended meaning is this:
since all dharmas are but the single mind, they are originally quiescent and do not require further extinction; therefore, it is said that "all things have no *nirvāṇa*.

However, since all dharmas are by nature primordially *nirvāṇa*, every phenomenon is authentic and entirely the true essence of the *dharmakāya*. Being thus, how could there be [any distinction between samsara and nirvana]?
Is *nirvāṇa* that which is realized by the Buddha? Therefore, it is said that there is neither *nirvāṇa* nor a Buddha. This refers to the eternal abiding of the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, how could there be a Buddha who further enters *nirvāṇa*? Why is this so? Because it is far removed from the subject of awakening (*buddhi*) and the object of awakening (*buddhya*).
That is to say, this absolute, non-dual single mind is fundamentally devoid of the opposition between subject and object. Only the Buddha realizes this; as for what is designated [as such], it is...
"Existence as if non-existent"—these two are both to be abandoned. Therefore, in both translations, the Yakṣa King first asks the Buddha: "How does one abandon what is dharmic?
How does one abandon what is non-dharmic? The Buddha replied: "The heterodox view it that birth and death constitute the Dharma."
Nirvāṇa is non-dharmic because both of these [existence and non-existence] should be abandoned. Mahāmati praised this, saying:
"To be free from both existence and non-existence is the essential purport of the entire sūtra. This does not extend beyond the single question initiated by the yakṣa and Mahāmati’s verse of praise.
Therefore, what is subsequently refuted below consists merely of the two views of existence and non-existence.

The *siddhānta* is beyond verbal expression. In the Sanskrit language, *siddhānta* means "universal bestowal" (*paryāpta-dāna*). This refers to the Buddha’s universal bestowal of four dharmas upon sentient beings. These four are:
first, the *loka-siddhānta*, which causes sentient beings to obtain the benefit of joy; second, the *pudgala-siddhānta*, which causes them to obtain the benefit of generating wholesome roots;
third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, which causes them to obtain the benefit of destroying evil; and fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.

*Siddhānta* (established tenets) brings about the benefit of enabling entry into the principle. This means that although the Buddha universally bestows the four methods upon sentient beings, he does so only in accordance with their individual capacities.
Fundamentally, these are beyond the characteristics of verbal expression. [The text] intends to reprove Mahāmati for failing to comprehend the purport of this transcendence of words.
Therefore, this question was asked. I have specifically manifested and established the principle of the numerical phrases that transcend words.
Thus, each subsequent item is said to be "not.
When Mahāmati heard that the True Suchness of the One Mind is free from all marks and utterly beyond verbal expression, he thereby came to know the ten dharma-realms.
All such characteristics are manifested solely by the mind and transformed solely by consciousness; they are matters pertaining to the gate of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, [the text] asks how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses. Regarding the "seven kinds of self-nature," the Wei translation states that non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) have seven kinds of self-nature.
The lecturers generally explain this using the principles of the orthodox teaching, which is a profound ignorance. Little do they realize that this sutra...

Because they exclusively refute the principle that all is mind-only and consciousness-only, the non-Buddhists establish a separate and distinct dharma, designating it as the "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*).
Because they fail to perceive the true cause of consciousness—that which is neither identical to nor different from the delusion of reality—they posit this "distinct cause.

As the Buddha previously censured the non-Buddhists for falling into the view of nihilism, he specifically set forth the five types of "distinct causes" for the dharmas they conceive; these are called "superior."
"Exquisite! Noble one! Sovereign! Timely! As minute as a mote of dust! These are the factors reckoned by non-Buddhists to be the causes of production.

Therefore, immediately following this, the false conceptualizations they establish are presented; each has a fixed determination, and taking "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) as their thesis, there are seven such [theses].
Having already departed from heterodox schools, the subsequent presentation of the orthodox teaching states: "I have seven kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The underlying structure of the scripture from beginning to end makes the Buddha’s words perfectly clear; yet those who are ignorant make arbitrary conjectures, which is a profound error.
If the seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*) have already established the correct doctrine, why would the seven kinds of ultimate truth be restated later in the text? Would this not be redundant?
Yes. Regarding the seven kinds of the ultimate realm of mind: the Buddha’s eye takes the dharma-realm of the one mind as its own object.
The realm of wisdom (*prajñā*) is that the light of wisdom is immeasurable, penetrating and illuminating even the most minute atoms of all lands. The realm of knowledge (*jñāna*) refers to—
The eyes refer to the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, which exhaustively penetrate the distinctions between the true and the false, and the holy and the ordinary.

"Seeing the realm" (the Tang edition reads "the two views of the realm") means simultaneously illuminating both extremes of the ultimate and the conventional. "Transcending the two views" means exhausting the Middle Way within the single mind.
"Transcending the realm of the ten stages" means reaching the ultimate limit of the causal gate at the final moment of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Thus, the Tathāgata...
Reaching the realm, one realizes the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the noble wisdom of self-awakening, the ocean of the ultimate fruit. The intent is this:

that which I have established is termed the equality of the single-mind *tathatā*. Through the two wisdoms, the Buddha’s insight perceives the two emptinesses and realizes *tathatā*, proceeding through the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samantabhadra*) until entering the ocean of the Buddha-fruit.
This is designated as a Dharma-gate, for it relies upon the first [of the three natures], the self-nature of nature (*svabhāva-svabhāva*).
Because it is established upon the mind of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-citta*), it does not share in the evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

These seven [stages] of the mind of ultimate meaning are presented solely to indicate the realm of the Buddha; they do not speak of the causal mind (*hetu-citta*). Were one to speak of the causal mind, one would lose the essential intent.

Question: Why is it said that the three kinds of consciousness constitute the result? Answer: Within the first three kinds of consciousness, the initial manifestation-consciousness (*nengxian shi*) arises due to ignorance (*avidyā*) perfuming True Suchness (*tathatā*), serving as the cause for the arising of the manifesting-consciousness (*xiangxi shi*).

The grasping of various objects (*viṣaya*) and so forth serves as the cause for the arising of the discriminating-object-consciousness (*fenbie shishi*). The Buddha’s intention was to clarify that this storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) relies upon True Suchness.
It arises through the union of the real and the false; therefore, the *ālayavijñāna* is specifically designated as the cause of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
This true cause is established in order to refute the non-causality and false causality of external paths, thereby distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox.

It points directly to the gate of contemplation wherein the mind alone is like an illusion, revealing the direct observation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to suddenly shatter fundamental ignorance and suddenly realize the One.
Since the mind is the ultimate, supreme fruit, the principle of "Mind-Only" is established here as appropriate to clarify the characteristics of the three kinds of consciousness.
Question: In the Chapter on Arising and Ceasing, Mahāmati first asked how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses, to which the Buddha replied:
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of consciousness; explained in detail, there are eight characteristics. Thus far, the brief exposition of the three kinds of consciousness is complete.

Then, Mahāmati again inquired regarding the detailed exposition of the eight characteristics, first recounting what the World-Honored One had taught concerning mind (citta), thought (manas), mentation (vijñāna), the five dharmas, and the self-nature (svabhāva) of characteristics, stating: "The sphere of practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is one's own mind."

Having shown that the objects of perception, such as the seen and so forth, are not in conjunction, and having revealed the heart of all Buddha-teachings—the true nature established by the single teaching—[the interlocutor] then requests an explanation of the ocean-like realm of the *ālayavijñāna* and the *dharmakāya*. Why is this? The answer is:
This is a general inquiry; its underlying currents are profound and hidden, making it most difficult to comprehend. Please allow me to attempt an explanation. Regarding this sutra:
It simply demonstrates that quiescent extinction is the one mind detached from all marks. Therefore, it is said: "The five dharmas and the three natures are all empty;

the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are both discarded. Thus, when Mahāmati first asked about the hundred and eight phrases, he questioned by way of the categories of the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
Consequently, the Buddha pointed to quiescent extinction as the one mind and answered directly. Hence, it is called "One."
All [these] are incorrect. This is the direct pointing to the one mind. Since not a single dharma is established, there is no room for verbal explanation.

This reveals that the *tathatā* of the one mind is free from all marks. Therefore, when Mahāmati subsequently asks how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses, this refers to the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind (*cittotpāda-nirodha-mukha*), wherein verbal explanation is permissible. However, within the gate of arising and ceasing, first...

Regarding the question on the various consciousnesses: since the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two kinds of selflessness are all established based on the transformation of the eight consciousnesses through these three gateways, he first asks about the single gateway of the various consciousnesses, before yet having asked about the meanings of the latter three gateways—the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two kinds of selflessness.
The Buddha’s answer states that, briefly stated, the various ālayavijñānas consist of three types of consciousness; [if] explained extensively...

There are eight aspects. Having already briefly answered by first explaining the three consciousnesses and fully revealing the self-substance of the eighth consciousness, Mahāmati requests again that these eight aspects be taught.
His question regarding the ocean-waves of the *ālayavijñāna* is, in fact, a question concerning the causes for the arising of the preceding seven consciousnesses.

However, his request begins by enumerating what has been discussed: the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*). This is because...

Regarding the phrase "attaining the realization of the true Buddha-mind," this serves as a general summary of the preceding questions and answers, articulating the understanding of the Buddha’s intent.

It refers back to the question concerning the arising of the seven consciousnesses. However, the statement that "the five dharmas, etc., are established based upon the eight consciousnesses" was the Buddha’s response:
"All are not [existent]. This already captures the Buddha’s revelation of the true Buddha-mind.

Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into the gate of arising and ceasing, the World-Honored One briefly explained three kinds of consciousness. The World-Honored One’s discourse on inconceivable perfuming and transformation is the very cause for the arising of the eight consciousnesses;
he further spoke of the "true consciousness" and the "manifesting consciousness," which refers to the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), that is, the Tathāgatagarbha.
I have already grasped this essential meaning. My thought is this: the five dharmas and so forth are all established based upon the eight consciousnesses, yet I do not know...
For what reason do the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses arise? Furthermore, not knowing how they arise is equivalent to their non-arising;

thus, he asks about the ocean-waves of the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the realm of the *dharmakāya*. Moreover, not knowing why the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the two forms of selflessness (*anātman*) are established, he requests an explanation of the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses and inquires into the meaning of the four gates. Therefore, the World-Honored One [responded].
Below, he first answers the reasons for the arising of the eight consciousnesses, and subsequently reiterates the questions regarding the five dharmas and the self-nature (*svabhāva*).

After the Buddha has answered each point individually, he concludes by returning to the contemplation of the two kinds of non-self (*anātman*), which constitutes the gateway to the contemplation of mind-only (*cittamātra*).
This is the true heart-essence of the Buddha’s word; therefore, the purport of these answers extends from this point through to the subsequent "Chapter on the Result. Thus, it is comprehensive.

By elucidating the five dharmas and the self-natures, and revealing correct wisdom and suchness, one fully exhausts the ultimate meaning of entering the gate of true suchness from the gate of birth-and-death.
This major outline is very clear; one should examine it comprehensively.
Question: Mahāmati asks about the ocean-like waves of the *ālayavijñāna*, yet he is inquiring about the first seven consciousnesses;
why then does he speak of the "realm of the Dharma-body"? Answer: Mahāmati is summarizing and taking to heart the principle of the One Mind. His intention is this:

the Buddha has previously stated that mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), mentation (*vijñāna*), the five dharmas, and the three natures are all empty; this is the very self-nature of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In the objective realm of the mind’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), not a single dharma is established; all oppositions are severed, and thus it is said to be "non-conjunction.

Having spoken thus, the true heart of the Buddha’s word has been revealed. This already captures the purport that the preceding consciousness-store (*ālayavijñāna*) and the Tathāgata-garbha are neither identical nor different in terms of their reality and falsity. However, the cause for the arising of the preceding seven consciousnesses is not yet known.
The eye has the meaning of being originally non-arising. Therefore, it is requested that you explain that the ocean-waves of the *ālayavijñāna* are precisely the realm of the *dharmakāya*.
Thus, in the subsequent answer, four causes and conditions are shown for the arising of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). The nature of the eye’s dependent arising is emptiness;

the eye manifests arising which is the very meaning of non-arising—this is the realm of the *dharmakāya*. Regarding the combination with the characteristics of karma-born [phenomena]: however, karma...

This refers to the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*). "Arising" refers to the ignorance of the characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*). The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Based on the *ālayavijñāna*, it is said that there is ignorance.

Initially, ignorance perfumes the True Suchness (*tathatā*) to produce the karmic consciousness. Once the karmic consciousness has been produced, the ignorance of the characteristic of arising then relies upon that karmic consciousness;

therefore, it is said that the characteristic of arising is conjoined with the karmic consciousness. Because the ignorance of the characteristic of arising perfumes the karmic consciousness, it consequently...
When a defiled mind arises, one deeply conceives of it as "self"; this is precisely the characteristic of the arising of the seventh consciousness.
In the verse on the eight consciousnesses, the Buddha reveals that the eight consciousnesses are themselves reality (*tathatā*); they are originally of one essence, being different yet not different.
He uses the metaphor of ocean waves and the *dharmakāya* to demonstrate this realm: just as he points to the ocean water and its waves, the waves are different while the water is not.
Mahāmati then used the sun and moon as a metaphor for the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, saying: "The Tathāgata should preach the Dharma of equality and reality to all sentient beings.
Why does the World-Honored One consistently teach the followers of the two vehicles that the six consciousnesses alone are the root of birth and death?
For what reason do you not preach that the eight consciousnesses are the true reality? The Buddha replied, "I am referring to them..."
The minds of sentient beings are not true; they are simply incapable of receiving the True Dharma, yet it is not that I do not teach it.
For example, the ten lines beginning with "the waves of the ocean" serve as a metaphor to reveal that this Dharma inherently possesses the distinction between sudden and gradual approaches;
thus, the teaching is established accordingly. Nevertheless, although the teaching has sudden and gradual aspects, in reality there is no fixed sequence. My intention is as follows: [I am]...

When explaining the gradual emergence of the six consciousnesses, it has never been done without simultaneously encompassing the eight consciousnesses; it is simply that sentient beings who hear this do not understand it.
Furthermore, the analogy of the painter is established: when the Eye of Wisdom expounds the Dharma, it should be established according to the sequence of the capacities of those beings.
The two lines regarding "the colors having no patterns" illustrate that the Dharma is fundamentally beyond words, yet it is employed merely to please sentient beings; it cannot be otherwise.
This was not established merely according to the circumstances; it is not that I am failing to speak the truth. The subsequent passage further clarifies this profound meaning:
it states that not only are provisional teachings said to be unreal, but even regarding the true teaching, there is no "real dharma" given to people.

This is because the true reality is free from names and words, and all things are like illusions. The final statement, "Even the śrāvakas do not possess [this portion]," serves as sufficient evidence.
Mahāmati harbors a doubt in his mind that the Buddha has not yet taught the true doctrine of the eight consciousnesses to those of the two vehicles.
"The Compassionate One" refers to the Buddha; it means that today he finally expounds the realm of self-realization.

The prose section concludes by indicating that if one wishes to know the realm of self-realization—the direct manifestation of one's own mind—one must engage in authentic practice and attain personal awakening;
it is not sufficient merely to explain it and then stop. Therefore, the subsequent text demonstrates the three characteristics of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

Answer: The Buddha’s intention is to manifest in general that there is only mind and no external objects. The five dharmas, the three natures, and the two absences of self arise from delusion;

Nevertheless, the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) predominates among the laity, while the grasping at phenomena predominates among those who study [the Dharma].
Those who practice the Buddha-dharma predominate. As for the view of self (*ātman*) described in the *Awakening of Faith*, it also arises based on what one has heard of the Buddha-dharma.

Question: Regarding the refutation of the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), the scriptural passages point to the meaning of the words and thus their intent is very clear.

However, if one takes the refutation of the attachment to self (*ātmagrāha*) to be based on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the underlying meaning remains unmanifest; Mahāmati merely asks about conceptual construction.

Answer: Generally speaking, when it is said that "discursive thought" (vikalpa) refers primarily to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), it is because for the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), such thought is merely incidental.

However, that which is conceptually grasped by the discursive thought of non-Buddhists is simply the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Although Mahāmati asked generally about the source from which discursive thought arises, the World-Honored One specifically pointed out that it consists of the grasper and the grasped (*grāhya-grāhaka*), falling into the views and attachments of existence and non-existence, and clinging to "self" and "mine."
That which is thus produced—this very object of deluded conceptualization—is the root of the self-clinging of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

As for ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who reckon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as the self, this was not explicitly revealed in the prose section of the sutra; however, when it comes to the verse, it says:

"The self of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is a designation; the various aggregates are the designation of the aggregates. The meaning here is perfectly clear. What further doubt could there be?

Question: Within the Mahāyāna teachings, it is universally taught that there are two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). These differ in being either conceptual (*vikalpita*) or innate (*sahaja*), and coarse or subtle.
It is said that the two conceptual graspings are completely severed from the stage of the three sages up to the first bhūmi.

As for the two innate graspings, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is completely severed from the second bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi, while the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is only exhausted upon reaching the Buddha-bhūmi. Now, this sutra speaks of the two [types of grasping], the coarse and the subtle...

[The questioner] said: "I grasp that [the afflictions] are severed and exhausted all at once, yet I do not yet understand its underlying meaning; I ask for a detailed explanation. He replied: "This sutra is the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Its intent lies in the sudden shattering of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the sudden realization of the one mind (*ekacitta*); therefore, the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*) are also severed all at once. The Great Sutra states:
'Because one does not comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is termed ignorance. This ultimate truth is precisely what this sutra..."
It is said that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the quiescence of the single mind. However, "not understanding" (*a-parijñāna*) refers precisely to ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Understanding" (*parijñāna*) means knowing. When the sūtras repeatedly speak of "knowing the manifestation of one's own mind," they mean understanding the mind of the ultimate truth.

Furthermore, the two obstacles—the coarse and the subtle—exist because of ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, to speak of the sudden realization of the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind is to suddenly shatter ignorance.
Once ignorance is shattered, from where could those two obstacles possibly arise?

Because the essence of the *mukhamaṇḍala* (the face of reality) possesses the meaning of the great light of wisdom, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). This is precisely the noble self-realized wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Furthermore, if the eye were identical to the mind’s correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), it would uniquely illuminate the essence of the single mind in its state of quiescent extinction, and thus all [delusions] would be transcended.
Now, because one does not understand this, false discrimination and attachment arise; therefore, it is called "false conceptualization" (*vikalpa*).

This sutra speaks of severing false conceptualization rather than merely severing ignorance. In the place where false conceptualization is purified, one immediately realizes the single mind; therefore, there is no [separate stage for severing ignorance].

It is merely a matter of gradual sequence. That is to say: "To know that which is illusory is itself to be free from it; no further expedient means are required. To be free from illusion is itself awakening;
there is likewise no gradual progression. Therefore, this is called the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Question: Regarding the chapter on transformation (*pariṇāma*), it is said that "transformation" refers to the condition of all sentient beings as they pass through birth and death, casting off one body and receiving another. Why, then, does it specifically point to external phenomena? Answer:

The Buddha taught that when sentient beings pass through birth and death and receive retributions—whether good or ugly—it is solely in accordance with the conditions of their wholesome or unwholesome karma. Therefore, he spoke of it being like milk turning into curd.
The ripening of wine, fruits, and so forth is merely a maturation that follows conditions.

Because externalists falsely imagine there to be a creator who acts as a transforming sovereign, they harbor such false views and conceptualizations; therefore, he specifically informs them, saying: "Such are the ignorant and foolish sentient beings."
They arise from the cultivation of one's own deluded imaginings. In reality, there is no dharma that acts as a sovereign over arising and ceasing; they merely arise as forms like illusions or dreams.
To say they "arise from the cultivation of one's own deluded imaginings" refers to false teachers and false teachings, which are but the grasping at a self through discrimination.
Based on what has been said thus far, this refers to the discrimination of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

A question is asked: In the Chapter on Continuity, Mahāmati, having heard the previous Buddha’s teaching on the characteristics of transformation (*pariṇāmalakṣaṇa*), immediately inquired into the meaning and nature of the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
While birth and death are summoned by the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), he inquired merely in terms of verbal expression; furthermore—
Why is it that the benefits of the ultimate fruit are cited for the sake of those who request [instruction]? The answer is: The purport of this sutra is profound and hidden;

it is by no means easily perceived by those of shallow understanding. This is because, as previously explained in the section on the awakening of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), the Buddha taught that one awakens to the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*), fully understands the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa-dvaya*), eliminates the two afflictions (*kleśa-dvaya*), and is liberated from the two kinds of death (*mṛtyu-dvaya*); this is what is called the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening.

In this section on the realization of abandonment, the true cause is revealed by means of destroying the two attachments and severing the two obstacles. However, regarding the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is spoken of as "attachment to phenomena" (*dharmagrāha*) solely in reference to attachment to verbal expression.

Thus, although Mahāmati poses his question in terms of verbal expression, the eleven continuities that constitute the answer are all attachments to verbal expression; these are designated as the cognitive obstacle.

As for those who designate the transformation-death (*pariṇāmika-maraṇa*) [as the object of abandonment], [it is because they fail to realize that such death is itself a product of attachment to verbal expression].
This refers to the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Because there are two types of hindrances, there are also two types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Therefore, at the conclusion, it is summarized that the three characteristics of the deluded person constitute the succession of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which invites innate self-grasping (*ātman-grāha*).

This summarizes both hindrances and both types of death, all of which are invited by the grasping of the seventh consciousness. Thus, the fault is attributed to the consciousness of attachment resulting from the conjunction of the three [factors].
This is the root of the continuous cycle of birth and death. The Buddha’s intention is very clear; it is simply that those of shallow understanding find it difficult to perceive.
A question is asked: When the World-Honored One spoke of the cessation of deluded consciousness as being called *nirvāṇa*, he also said that the seven consciousnesses do not arise.
Now, why do you say that both types of grasping arise simultaneously and attribute the fault to the seven consciousnesses? Is this not a contradiction of your own words? The answer is:
When observing the Buddha’s established teachings, each statement has its own specific referent; they are not contradictory.

For the former [passage] states that because the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is blown by the winds of objective conditions, the waves of the preceding seven consciousnesses arise—this refers to their arising and ceasing. Now, [the present passage] reveals the intrinsic nature of the *ālayavijñāna*.
The nature is originally nirvāṇa. However, because it is stirred by the winds of objective realms, there is birth and death.
If it were not stirred by the winds of objective realms, its own nature would be eternally abiding nirvāṇa. Now, these objective realms are the realms of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Furthermore, these sensory objects are merely manifestations of the mind; they are inherently suchness (*tathatā*). If the six consciousnesses do not grasp or cling through攀緣 (*pán-yuán*, objective attachment), then—
All phenomena are suchness, immovable. However, because the six consciousnesses do not realize that all is but mind, they falsely engage in攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to objects) and grasping.

Thus, the winds of consciousness fan and stir, blowing back upon the ocean of the storehouse-consciousness and giving rise to the seven waves. This is what is meant by the arising of the wind of objective conditions.
All of this is the fault of the six consciousnesses; the seventh consciousness is not involved, because this consciousness functions by relying on the internal door.
Therefore, it is said that [the seventh] does not arise. This is why, when the six consciousnesses are extinguished, the eighth consciousness is the nirvāṇa of its own nature.

Now, regarding the statement that the two types of innate grasping are attributed to the fault of the seventh consciousness: this refers to the fact that from time immemorial, the seventh consciousness has functioned exclusively as a single entity.

To grasp the eight consciousnesses as a self is called "the storehouse of self-love and grasping" (*ātmagrāha-ālaya*). To gather all seeds and continue the cycle of birth and death is called "the continuity of rebirth.
That this continues uninterrupted throughout long kalpas is the capacity of this [eighth] consciousness, while the six consciousnesses do not participate therein.

This is because it is the six consciousnesses that perform karma, the eighth consciousness that receives retribution, and the seventh consciousness alone that maintains the continuity of birth and death. Thus it is.
Each [statement] is spoken according to its predominant capacity; it is not a fault of internal contradiction between preceding and succeeding words.
Question: In the sūtra, throughout each section, Mahāmati’s questions frequently cite the fruits and virtues as a request.

Yet, the World-Honored One has already concluded and manifested these fruits and virtues more than once. What, then, is the distinction between this and the direct manifestation of the fruits and virtues?
The answer is: O Mahāmati, regarding what was previously stated in the sequential questions as "fruit" (*phala*), this was intended as a request for the teaching of the benefits of the Dharma;

it specifically cites the fruit to manifest the benefit of the Dharma. When the World-Honored One speaks of the "virtue of the fruit," this is for the purpose of refuting the heterodox and clarifying the true cause.

By citing the name of the fruit to provide verification of the true cause, all of these pertain to the gate of the cause (*hetu-dvāra*) and do not constitute a formal exposition of the virtue of the fruit itself.
Now, because practice is perfected, the two obstacles have been shattered, the five stages of dwelling have been extinguished, and one is forever free from the two types of death;

having returned to the ultimate single mind, the cause is exhausted and the fruit is fulfilled. This title reveals the ultimate fruit of the single mind of perfection. This is the formal exposition of the fruit-virtues.

It explains the two transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) to reveal that the Dharma-body emerges from its entanglements and realizes the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This...
This is the ultimate principle of returning to the truth by reversing delusion.

In the fourth fascicle below, a question is asked: "One should clarify that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding; it is the state where birth-and-death and nirvana are equal. To reverse delusion and return to the truth [is to transcend] karma..."
Having already reached the ultimate realization of the true source of the one mind, Mahāmati then asked: "What is meant by 'momentary' (*kṣaṇika*)? He replied:

"This is precisely the fundamental principle that traces the beginning and concludes with the end, returning to the ultimate norm of the one mind. It is because [the Buddha] first addressed the hundred and eight meanings."

The Buddha, with eyes serene and mind unified in *samādhi*, replied that "all things are non-existent. Thereupon, Mahāmati asked how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses.
Thus, delusion and enlightenment, as well as cultivation and realization, are all matters within the gate of arising and ceasing.

However, Mahāmati’s initial inquiry into the one hundred and eight meanings comprehensively encompasses the ten realms, including the environment and its inhabitants, delusion and enlightenment, cause and effect; it does not go beyond these five [categories].
The Dharma is fully encompassed by the three self-natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of non-self; these four categories exhaust all phenomena.

Therefore, by now investigating and interrogating various delusions to realize the One Mind, it is shown that the five dharmas and the three self-natures are all empty, and both the eight consciousnesses and the two non-selves are discarded.
Ultimately, one returns to the true source of the One Mind to manifest the ultimate limit of the Dharmakāya, demonstrating that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are equal.

These [states] represent the return from delusion to awakening; they are collectively subsumed under the category of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). None of them transcend the two kinds of arising and ceasing initially questioned by Mahāmati.

This means that because there are the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, there exist the biased and erroneous attachments of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the Two Vehicles.
Because there are the continuous flows (*pravṛtti*) of arising, abiding, and ceasing, there exist bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage.
This view intends to clarify that even if one realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), one has not yet departed from the deluded perception of arising and ceasing. As it is said:

"When the mind of Bodhi arises, the mind of arising and ceasing ceases; yet this still belongs to arising and ceasing. Now, the meaning is revealed that arising and ceasing are fundamentally non-arising and non-ceasing.
If one understands that they are fundamentally non-arising and non-ceasing, then all that was previously stated is merely a matter of dreams—occurring within the midst of deluded effort.

There is indeed that which is cultivated and severed. Therefore, the previous metaphor of crossing a river in a dream illustrates that all cultivation and realization are the Dharma-gate of dreams and illusions;

only then does it reveal the ultimate pinnacle of the Dharmakāya. By this, it is clearly seen that our Buddha’s teaching from beginning to end does not utter a single word—this is the ultimate pinnacle of the Sudden School.
Supplement to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* (End)
